abstract: Census Bureau Business Trends and Outlook Survey, biweekly cycle 202623, published November 19, 2026, reference period October 19 to November 1, 2026. National AI use reached 25.0 percent of firms (SE 0.60 percent), the highest reading in the series and its first at or above 25 percent, up 0.8 points from 24.2 percent in cycle 202622. This is the second cycle to field the three AI follow-up questions introduced in cycle 202622 under Federal Register notice FR Doc. 2026-18304 (Q8 employee generative-SI use, Q9 AI's effect on total headcount, Q10 AI's effect on new hires), so for the first time those questions have a prior reading to compare against. It is also the cycle that settles whether the response-quality shift seen in cycle 202622 was a blip: it was not. Values are dated to reference-period end, which for BTOS falls two to three weeks before publication.
keyFindings: National AI use was 25.0 percent of firms (SE 0.60 percent) for the two weeks ending 2026-11-01, up from 24.2 percent (SE 0.61 percent) for the cycle ending 2026-10-18 and 24.6 percent (SE 0.27 percent) for the cycle ending 2026-10-04. The 0.8-point rise is about one standard error of the difference and is not individually significant, but 25.0 percent is the series high and the first reading at or above 25 percent.

The response-quality shift that appeared with cycle 202622 held rather than reverting. 'Do not know' on Q7 was 13.3 percent against 13.9 percent one cycle before and 9.6 percent two cycles before; 'No' was 61.6 percent against 61.9 percent and 65.8 percent; the standard error on the yes share was 0.60 percent against 0.61 percent and 0.27 percent. Two consecutive cycles at the new level indicate a level shift that arrived with the new follow-up questions, not one-cycle noise. Practically, cycle-to-cycle comparisons from 202622 onward are sound, but standard errors from 202621 and earlier are not comparable with them.
Q28, the six-month expectation of SI/AI use, was 28.2 percent (SE 0.52 percent), up from 27.6 percent and close to the 28.6 percent of cycle 202621.

Q8, second reading: 27.6 percent of AI-using businesses (SE 0.57 percent) report employees using generative SI to assist in work-related tasks, against 58.8 percent no and 13.6 percent do not know. Up from 26.8 percent (SE 0.56 percent), a move of about one standard error of the difference.

Q9, second reading: among AI-using businesses, AI's effect on total headcount over the prior six months was an increase for 7.3 percent (SE 0.52 percent), a decrease for 2.4 percent, no change for 87.4 percent and unknown for 2.9 percent, against 6.6 / 2.5 / 87.3 / 3.6 percent in the first reading. Firms reporting gains now outnumber those reporting losses by about three to one.

Q10, second reading: AI's effect on the number of new employees hired was an increase for 2.3 percent, a decrease for 3.0 percent, no change for 91.2 percent and unknown for 3.5 percent, against 2.5 / 3.3 / 90.2 / 4.1 percent. The sign asymmetry between Q9 and Q10 found in the first cycle repeats: on existing headcount more AI-using firms report a rise than a fall, on new hiring slightly more report a fall than a rise. Two readings is not a trend, but it is no longer a single observation.

Sector detail (Sector.xlsx, same cycle, Q7 yes share): Information 49.6 percent from 45.0 percent, Educational Services 44.0 percent from 39.5 percent, Finance and Insurance 42.7 percent from 39.2 percent, Professional, Scientific and Technical Services 40.8 percent from 41.6 percent, Real Estate 35.1 percent from 28.2 percent, Health Care 25.3 percent from 24.6 percent. Information is within half a point of half of all firms; Educational Services and Real Estate posted the largest single-cycle gains. Mining, Utilities and Agriculture are suppressed ('S') this cycle.
methodology: Biweekly establishment survey across a large national sample of about 1.2 million US businesses split into six panels, published as an experimental data product. Each estimate is collected over a two-week window covering the preceding two-week reference period; cycle 202623 was collected 2026-11-02 to 2026-11-15 for the reference period 2026-10-19 to 2026-11-01 and published 2026-11-19. Q7 and Q28 are asked of all respondents. Q8, Q9 and Q10 are asked only of respondents who answered yes to Q7, under skip logic introduced to limit respondent burden; Q8's 27.6 percent exceeding Q7's 25.0 percent confirms the subpopulation denominator arithmetically. The November 2025 rewording from AI use 'in producing goods or services' to 'in any business function', and the October 2026 relabelling of AI as SI, are both same-construct instrument changes, and Census publishes one continuous series.
qualifiers: Q7 is a firm-level adoption share, not a measure of how much work AI performs, and counts any use in the prior two weeks. Q8 through Q10 are firm-reported, conditional on AI use, and unweighted by firm size, so they describe the share of AI-using establishments rather than the share of employment or of jobs affected; they cannot be read as a displacement rate and belong on the displacement charts as overlays rather than data points. Q9 and Q10 ask about the prior six months while the cycle's reference period is two weeks, so their window does not match the biweekly series. The single-cycle rise to 25.0 percent is inside sampling error and should not be read as acceleration on its own; what is new is the series high, not a significant move. Standard errors on Q7 remain at roughly double their pre-202622 level, so recent cycles carry wider uncertainty than the earlier series suggests. Sector-level values rest on much smaller cells than the national figure and several sectors are suppressed. The biannual AI Supplement, linked as a 'Questionnaire with SI Supplement', remains a separate instrument with an 11-week reference window and should not be treated as the latest point in this series. The AI questions appear in every cycle; the press releases are boilerplate and never mention AI, so the National.xlsx workbook is the only reliable read.
